title: Strict free choice concerns means and what is in our power, and includes indifference
source_text: XXIII. Strictius vero usurpata libertas, sive liberum arbitrium restringitur, ipsis fatentibus ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, & versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, circa ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & recte ab Aristotele definitur spontaneum ex praevia deliberatione ortum, sive Deliberativa appetitio eorum quae sunt in nostra potestate. Quo in sensu liberi actus dicuntur qui sunt mere contingentes, & qui a nobis pro arbitrio fieri possunt, aut non fieri. Eoque respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, neque aliter voluntas libera est quam quatenus est indifferens, nempe, cum possit circa idem objectum agere, vel non agere, & cum possit tam illud, quam aliud, aut ejus oppositum eligere. Et hoc sensu Deus libere se non amat, quia naturae necessitate seipsum vult & amat; nec etiam homo libere vult esse foelix, & non vult esse miser, quia sic vult & non aliter per naturalem quandam necessitatem.
pass_a_gloss: But liberty used more strictly, or free choice is restricted, by their own admission to means related to the end, or to those things which conduce little, or nothing to the end, & is occupied about ta eph' hemin, that is, about those things which are in our power, & is rightly defined by Aristotle the spontaneous arisen from previous deliberation, or Deliberative appetition of those things which are in our power. In which sense those acts are called free which are merely contingent, & which can be done by us at our choice, or not be done. And in that respect liberty includes a certain indifference, nor is the will otherwise free than inasmuch as it is indifferent, namely, since it can act about the same object, or not act, & since it can choose as well this, as another, or its opposite. And in this sense God does not love himself freely, because by necessity of nature he wills & loves himself; nor also does man freely will to be happy, & not will to be miserable, because he so wills & not otherwise by a certain natural necessity.
pass_b_english: Freedom in the stricter sense, or free choice, is by their own admission limited to means directed to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to it. It concerns ta eph' hemin, the things in our power, and Aristotle rightly defines it as the spontaneous arising from prior deliberation, or deliberative desire for things in our power.

In this sense acts are called free when they are purely contingent and we can do them or not do them as we choose. Taken so, freedom includes a kind of indifference. The will is free only in so far as it is indifferent, that is, able to act or not act toward the same object, and able to choose this, or something else, or its opposite.

In this sense God does not love himself freely, since he wills and loves himself by the necessity of his nature. Nor does man freely want to be happy and not want to be miserable, since he wills this, and cannot will otherwise, by a natural necessity.

lemmas.gloss: ta eph' hemin, the things in our power

choices.why: The technical term for the will's openness to either alternative is kept, as in the earlier theses.
